title: PayCheck Sui
tagline: One agent gets burned. Every other agent is warned.
intro: PayCheck Sui checks a Sui address before an AI agent pays it. When one agent pays an address and the money goes bad, it writes that down in shared memory on Walrus. The next agent about to pay a different address run by the same people gets stopped, even though it has never seen either address before.

bench.columnsHonest: I also gave the plain AI the same report that memory holds, pasted into its prompt. It stopped as many group wallets as memory did. So memory isn't winning on smarter reasoning. It wins because the report is shared, it stays, and every agent reads it without anyone pasting it in. A stronger model might do better than this small one, and you can run it with --model=<name>. The stronger models on my key were over quota or capped at 20 calls a day.
bench.lossesHeading: Where the checker with memory got it wrong or did worse
bench.lossesLead: Four of the held-back cases, as they came out:

losses.text: The AI said "do not pay". The checker found the shared fee payer and said "pay". The wallet reported as bad has a different fee payer in the checker's reading, so the report was saved under another address and memory found nothing for this wallet.
An ordinary wallet that sent money back to whoever funded it. The checker said "caution" and the AI said "pay".
The AI named the wallet that funded this group. The checker didn't, though memory still stopped the payment.
The checker found no link and said "pay". The shared transactions aren't in the oldest 50 it reads.

limits.heading: What this is not, and where it's weak
items: It's not a fraud detector. Being linked to other wallets isn't a sign of danger, because exchanges and payroll wallets fund lots of honest people. A red answer needs a stored report of a bad payment that reaches the address through a real link.
It can't protect the first victim of a brand new group. Until someone reports a bad payment, the answer is "pay, linked, no bad history" and the links are only shown.
It reads only the oldest 50 transactions of a wallet. On a busy wallet that can hide a link. It missed 2 of the 20 real groups, and one of those misses was for exactly this reason.
Shared services are spotted with a rule I picked: 15 or more wallets over 25 hours or more. I checked those two numbers against real data, but I haven't proven they're right.
One bad report is enough to turn a direct link red. Every answer shows who made the report and its memory id, so you can judge the source yourself.
The real set has small groups (2 to 9 wallets) and young ordinary wallets. It shows the method works on real chain data. It doesn't show it works everywhere.
Ankr keeps less history for an address than Tatum does, so some links are checked one transaction at a time instead of through the address history.

footer: PayCheck Sui, built for the Tatum and Walrus Memory hackathon. Sui data from Tatum, second opinion from Ankr, memory on Walrus Memory.
